items.entity: square design domain (side length and out-of-plane thickness)
items.description: Results, Compliance minimization (Fig. 2a): the text only says 'a square domain is divided evenly by a 4×4 mesh'. No side length or thickness is given. The 1:1 aspect ratio is fixed, so size and thickness only scale the energy, and Ẽ is normalized by E(ρ_O) anyway.
readings: Any physical size, e.g. 1 m × 1 m with thickness 0.01 m

items.entity: downward force at the 'top right edge'
items.description: Results: 'A force downward is applied at the top right edge'. This could mean the top-right corner (on the symmetry line, as in a mirrored half-MBB beam), the end of the top boundary next to that corner, or the top of the right (symmetry) boundary. The exact spot is shown only in Fig. 2a.
readings: Top-right corner node (x = L, y = L)
Top boundary next to the corner: x ∈ [0.75L, L], y = L (the rightmost element edge)
Upper end of the right/symmetry boundary: x = L, y ∈ [0.75L, L]

items.entity: downward force: point load vs distributed load
items.description: The text never says whether the force is a point load or a line traction, or how long the loaded segment is. 'Edge' suggests a segment, but the stated equivalence to minimizing 'the vertical displacement where the external force is applied' suggests a single point. Only Fig. 2a shows it.
readings: Concentrated point force at a single node
Uniform line traction over one element edge (length L/4) ending at the corner, split between that edge's two nodes

items.description: No force value is given anywhere. The text also doesn't say whether a load on the symmetry plane is the full load or half of it. Because the problem is linear and Ẽ = E/E(ρ_O) is a ratio, this only scales the result.
readings: F = 0.5 (half of a unit full-beam load, because of the symmetry plane)

items.entity: roller support at the 'bottom left edge'
items.description: Results: 'the bottom left edge is set as a roller (no vertical displacement)'. The support type is clear (u_y = 0, u_x free). What is unclear is whether only the bottom-left corner point is held or a segment of the bottom boundary. Only Fig. 2a shows the extent.
readings: Bottom-left corner node only (x = 0, y = 0), u_y = 0
Bottom boundary segment of the bottom-left element: x ∈ [0, 0.25L], y = 0, u_y = 0 on its two nodes

items.description: Eq. (6) uses Y0 but never gives a value. If ε is taken relative to Y0, it only scales the energy, and Ẽ is a ratio.
Poisson's ratio is not given anywhere for the compliance problems. It changes the shape of the elastic stiffness, not just its size.

items.entity: void stiffness ε in the SIMP law (Eq. 6)
items.description: Eq. (6) only says 'ε is a small number to avoid numerical singularity'. No value is given, and it isn't said whether ε is absolute or relative to Y0.

items.entity: 2D elasticity assumption (plane stress vs plane strain)
items.description: The problem is a 2D square solved in COMSOL 5.4 (Methods), but the text never says plane stress or plane strain. COMSOL's 2D Solid Mechanics default is plane strain, while typical TO codes use plane stress. The choice changes the effective Poisson's ratio.

items.entity: FE element type/order on the 4×4 mesh
items.description: Methods: FEM runs in COMSOL 5.4 on a mesh 'the same as the design variables' (4×4 elements, 25 nodes). The displacement interpolation order and the quadrature are not stated. On a mesh this coarse, bilinear and quadratic elements give very different bending stiffness, which can change the optimum and the reference value Ẽ = 0.293.
readings: Quadratic 8-node serendipity quads (likely the COMSOL Solid Mechanics default)

items.entity: mapping of the 25 nodal design variables to element stiffness
items.description: Results says ρ(x) is 'interpolated linearly by the nodal values of the element' and that SIMP (Eq. 6) is applied point by point. Methods says bilinear interpolation (Eq. 17). The quadrature used to integrate Y(ρ(x)) is not given, and a structured-grid solver normally uses one constant density per element. The caption's '5×5 design variables', together with Methods' 'meshes of FEM are the same as the design variables', could also be read as a 5×5 element grid.
readings: 4×4 elements; bilinear nodal density, with SIMP evaluated at each Gauss point
4×4 elements; element density = mean of its 4 nodal values, then SIMP
5×5 element grid with one constant density per design variable
Finer FE grid (e.g. 40×40) with element densities sampled from the bilinear 5×5 nodal field

items.description: Eq. (5) and Methods call w 'the vector of linear Gaussian quadrature' and say Σ w_i ρ_i is a 'weighted average' equal to 0.5. The nodal weights are never written out, and they decide how much edge and corner nodes count toward the volume.
readings: Normalized exact integral of the bilinear field: corner nodes 1/64, edge nodes 1/32, interior nodes 1/16
Uniform weights of 1/25 (plain mean of the nodal values)

items.description: No filter is mentioned for the compliance problems or their MMA benchmark. The only filter in the paper is a Helmholtz filter (radius = half the spacing between design points), used for the heat-problem 'Approximated' baseline. Standard TO solvers need a filter type and radius.
readings: No filter (bilinear nodal interpolation is the only regularization)
Helmholtz PDE filter with radius = half the nodal spacing (L/8)

items.entity: optimizer start and parameters for the gradient benchmark (Fig. 2d)
items.description: Methods gives only MMA via COMSOL with an optimality tolerance of 0.001. The initial density field, move limits and iteration cap are not given, and they can decide which local optimum is reached.
readings: Uniform initial ρ = 0.5 (equal to ρ_O and feasible)
Random feasible start, generated like SOLO's initial batch (uniform random values rescaled to a weighted average of 0.5)
